opus-5.5.text:
I think it starts from a pretty simple observation: the physical world doesn't happen in single frames. When a robot picks up a cup, opens a drawer, or folds a towel, what matters is how things change, how forces play out over time, what happens after you push something, and how objects respond. A single image tells you what's there. It doesn't tell you what's about to happen.

For a long time much of robot learning leaned on static perception. You recognize the object, estimate its pose, and then plan. That works in structured settings, but it breaks down once you get into messy, contact-rich, real-world manipulation. The robot needs some intuition about dynamics, a sense of cause and effect. Humans build that intuition by watching and interacting with the world continuously, not by looking at snapshots.

Video is the most natural carrier of that kind of knowledge. It contains motion, physics, intention, and the order in which actions unfold. There's also the scale argument. Robot data is expensive and slow to collect. You need hardware, teleoperation, and resets, and you end up with maybe thousands of hours if you're lucky. Video of humans and the world doing things is available at a scale that's orders of magnitude larger. So if a model can learn temporal structure from video, how the world evolves and what a reasonable next state looks like, that becomes a very strong prior. Then the robot-specific data only has to teach the last mile: how to map that understanding onto its own body and actions.

Coming from a background in generative modeling, I find this especially compelling. If a model can generate a plausible continuation of a video, it has implicitly learned something about how the world works. Coherent motion and consistent objects are hard to fake without some internal model of dynamics. So we started asking whether that generative, temporal understanding could serve as the foundation for action, a kind of world model the robot can reason with, rather than treating vision as a pure recognition problem.

Of course there are real challenges. Video doesn't come with action labels, the embodiment is different, and visual plausibility isn't the same as physical correctness. But directionally, I believe that if we want robots that generalize in the open world, they need to understand time, and video is where that understanding lives.

r001.rationale: It says the physical world unfolds over time and robots must handle changing states, forces, and object responses during actions such as manipulation; this makes temporal understanding necessary.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a single image or static perception with video’s motion, causal changes, and action sequence, clearly distinguishing temporal learning from independent-frame treatment.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer directly as the guest.

Honestly, it came from a frustration with how we were doing things before. For a long time, the whole field treated perception as a sequence of still images. You take a frame, you detect objects, you estimate pose, and then you feed that into a planner. But a robot doesn't live in snapshots. The world keeps moving while it's deciding, and more importantly, the robot itself is the one causing things to change.

So the question we kept running into was: where does a model learn what "cause and effect" looks like physically? If you push a cup, it slides, maybe it tips. If you let go of something, it falls. None of that is in a single image. It only exists in the transition between frames. And that transition, that temporal structure, is exactly the thing a robot needs to predict before it acts.

Video is also just the largest source of this kind of data that humans have ever produced. We have billions of hours of people doing ordinary things with their hands, in kitchens, in workshops, in factories. Nobody labeled it for robotics, but the physics and the intent are all embedded in how things unfold over time. It felt almost wasteful not to use it.

The other piece is that I come from generative modeling. When you train a video generation model well, you notice that it starts to get things like object permanence, contact, and plausible motion roughly right, without anyone telling it the rules. That was a strong hint to me. If a model can imagine what happens next in a scene, then it already has a kind of world model. The leap to robotics is asking: can we make that imagination conditional on the robot's own actions, so the robot can mentally rehearse before it moves?

So the decision wasn't really "video is trendy." It was that time is the dimension where physics, intention, and consequence all show up together, and video was the only medium that captures all three at scale.

r001.rationale: It says the world changes while a robot decides and that the robot’s own actions cause changes, so it must predict those transitions before acting.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the field’s sequence of still-image perception with temporal structure in transitions between video frames.

astra-6.text:
Because a robot has to understand how things change, not just what a scene looks like at one moment. A single image might show a hand next to a cup, but it doesn’t tell you whether the hand is reaching for it, picking it up, or putting it down. The sequence matters.

Video gives us a way to learn those transitions: how objects move, how interactions unfold, and what tends to happen next. For a robot, that’s essential. It needs to connect its current observation with an action and anticipate how that action could change the world.

r001.rationale: It says robots must connect current observations to actions and anticipate how those actions change the world, making temporal understanding necessary for acting.

r002.rationale: It contrasts what a single image can show with the transitions and sequence learned from video, communicating that frames must be understood over time rather than in isolation.

sol-6.1.text: Because a robot needs to understand how the world changes, not just what it looks like at a single moment. An image can show a hand next to a cup, but it doesn’t tell you whether the hand is reaching for it, picking it up, or putting it down. Video provides that temporal information—the order of events and how actions unfold. We wanted robots to learn from those changes so they could move beyond recognizing a scene toward understanding actions and anticipating what might happen next.

r001.rationale: It says robots need to understand how the world changes and actions unfold, but does not connect temporal modeling to robots needing to act in their environment.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a single image with video’s event order, but does not distinguish temporal learning from treating extracted video frames as independent images.
